newsitem.title: UK: EMERGING MARKET OUTLOOK - US outweighs Russia,Brazil.
newsitem.headline: EMERGING MARKET OUTLOOK - US outweighs Russia,Brazil.

text.p: Emerging market fortunes will hang once again on the U.S. interest rate story this week, though trade figures in Brazil and the prospect of a cabinet reshuffle in Russia will add spice to individual markets.

U.S. payroll figures that emerged higher than expected on Friday have taken some of the heat off emerging debt and equity markets in the short term at least. But investors remain nervous ahead of U.S. retail sales and inflation figures this week.
"The markets are more interested in (U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan) Greenspan and U.S. rates than in Russia or Brazil," said one emerging market strategist here.

Increasing expectations of a U.S. rate rise put a halt to the prolonged rally in emerging equities last week and depressed the emerging debt market, though Brady bonds and emerging market stocks recovered some ground on the back of Friday's better than anticipated data.
But many investors are taking no chances and will sit on the sidelines until the March 25 FOMC meeting -- the next opportunity at which U.S. rates can rise.
RUSSIA players at least will be looking for word on an expected cabinet reshuffle following the appointment on Friday of reformist Anatoly Chubais to the post of first deputy prime minister.
Analysts said the move had boosted prospects for Russian investors, but some said they were beginning to doubt whether any reshuffle would take place.

"All this could be part of the same rumour story," said David Mars, director of emerging European economics research at SBC Warburg, pointing to previous talk of high level oustings that eventually did not take place.
"Boris will be drawing attention to the fact that he's back," added another economist, referring to President Boris Yeltsin's wish to reassert himself after recent ill health.
Russia, gearing up for the launch of a jumbo mark Eurobond, said on Friday it planned to launch the deal this week.

Deutsche Bank officials in Frankfurt confirmed on Monday that the deal would go ahead as planned, adding the launch time had not been determined. Last week joint lead manager Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said the issue could be delayed until market conditions improved.

Ondine Smulders, Latin American equity strategist at HSBC James Capel, said trade figures due in BRAZIL on Tuesday were the single most important factor for that region's markets, apart from developments on the U.S. interest rate front.

"The market is going to be nervous until those numbers are reported," she said. Investors fear an extra-large figure for February, exacerbated by the inclusion of oil import data from energy giant Petrobras that was omitted from January's data.

In TURKEY, bottom-up equity investors -- who focus on particular companies rather than taking a "top down" macro-economic view -- will be out bargain-hunting this week after last week's 8.9 percent fall on the IFC investable index.
The spiral was prompted by the army's demand that the ruling islamist government clamp down on religious activism.
But Unal Kurtaran, director of Middle Eastern sales at Salomon Brothers in London, said he did not expect last week's crisis to lead to an early election.

"There will be speculation but I don't think there'll be early elections," he said. "You can expect bottom up fund managers to come in this week -- bottom-up stock picking will continue but top down investors will have to wait."
Investors are also keeping watch for an expected rating revision from Moody's Investor Services after Turkey's recent downgrade from rival agency Standard & Poor's.

Rumours of a second 25 basis point interest rate cut in CHILE, possibly as early as this week, means local pension funds will be gearing up for a switch out of fixed income and into the local equity market for healthier returns.
But foreign investors are likely to move first.

"Foreigners will start buying in anticipation of a rate cut and of the local pension funds moving into the market -- the local pension funds themselves won't move until you've seen the rate actually come down," said Ondine Smulders, Latin American strategist at HSBC James Capel.
"Probably the first rate cut (four weeks ago) wasn't enough, but a second cut should really trigger a movement from the fixed income to the equity market."

Rumours that announced tariff increases for VENEZUELA's telecoms firm CANTV would not be implemented conspired with a deal last month on wage increases to knock six percent of Venezuelan stocks last week.
"People will be disappointed if the tariff rise doesn't happen," Smulders said. "Lots of funds are cutting their weightings in Venezuela."
In eastern Europe, prospects of IMF deals for BULGARIA and ROMANIA will keep investors on tenterhooks.
"Both are getting close to IMF deals -- if Romania publishes a letter of intent, that will be very positive," said SBC Warburg's Mars.
Romania, which plans to discuss its 1997 state budget draft on Tuesday, is planning to lauch a 500 to 700 million mark bond this month, with a dollar-denominated or global issue to follow.
Hopes are running high meanwhile that BULGARIA will conclude an IMF deal this week, enabling it to set up a currency board to help stabilise its crumbling economy and repay foreign debts.
Elsewhere SRI LANKA is readying a $50 million floating rate note -- its first international debt issue since 1982 -- for possible launch this week.
The IFC emerging market composite investable index, IFC/IPRD, denominated in dollars, was off 1.2 percent week-on-week on Friday at 327.86.

Latin America was down 0.6 percent week-on-week at 626.17, Asia was down 0.8 at 265.76, and Europe, Middle East and Africa as a region was down 2.9 percent at 156.16. --London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
